The House of Tudor. Ruling England from 1485 to 1603, the Tudors emerged from the chaos of the Wars of the Roses to establish one of history's most celebrated dynasties. Tudor monarchs, especially Henry VIII and Elizabeth I, transformed England into a major European power, severed its ties with Rome, and made it a center of Renaissance learning and culture.

Henry VII founded the dynasty in 1485 by defeating Richard III at the Battle of Bosworth Field, ending the Wars of the Roses. His son, Henry VIII, reigned from 1509 to 1547 and broke with Rome over his marriage to Catherine of Aragon. He established the Church of England and made himself Supreme Head. He married six times and executed two queens. The English Reformation under Tudor rule severed England's Catholic ties and reshaped religion and politics for centuries to come.

Elizabeth I, the last Tudor monarch, reigned from 1558 to 1603. She restored Protestantism, defeated the Spanish Armada, and presided over England's golden age—a period of literature, exploration, and emerging power. The Tudors patronized the English Renaissance, and William Shakespeare wrote his greatest works under Elizabethan rule. The dynasty consolidated royal power over the nobility after the Wars of the Roses, establishing strong centralized governance.

When Elizabeth died, the Scottish House of Stuart inherited the English throne, ending the Tudor line.
